newsitem.title: USA: Clinton, Hashimoto set for "sushi summit".
newsitem.headline: Clinton, Hashimoto set for "sushi summit".

text.p: President Bill Clinton's summit with Japanese Prime Minister Ruytaro Hashimoto on Friday will be a lot like sushi -- full of tasty tidbits but thin on substance.

Unlike most previous summits between U.S. and Japanese leaders in recent years, there are no major trade differences to be ironed out, although U.S. officials are concerned about a rising trade imbalance with Japan after a period of decline.

Strains arising from the U.S. troop presence in Japan, which nearly reached breaking point after the 1995 rape of a schoolgirl by U.S. servicemen on Okinawa, have eased a great deal since a new security agreement was signed last year.

It is even unlikely that the name of Clinton's new envoy to Tokyo will be announced during the summit, although sources close to former Democratic House Speaker Tom Foley say he will be nominated to replace former Vice President Walter Mondale.

"There's no huge piece of broken crockery to be fixed or big problem to be overcome," a U.S. official said. "I think there's going to be more to the summit than meets the eye, but there's no formal document...associated with it."

Japanese Ambassador Kunihiko Saito said that while Clinton and Hashimoto did not have to negotiate anything, "we believe it is very important to have frequent exchanges of views on the highest level between our two countries."
Hashimoto arrives in Washington on Thursday night, meets Clinton the next morning and joins him afterward at a joint news conference. He meets Vice President Al Gore on Saturday.
The Clinton-Hashimoto meeting will be their fourth, and White House spokesman Mike McCurry said the two leaders enjoy "a very easygoing and comfortable personal relationship."

"As they often do, they will look at all aspects of the bilateral relationship, centering specifically on security issues and regional political issues. There will be, as always, some discussion of economic issues, although unlike previous encounters...that's not likely to dominate the discussions," McCurry said.

Saito said the prime minister was likely to brief Clinton on his economic policies, which are designed to pull Japan out of recession. Hashimoto "is now carrying out a very broad reform programme," the Japanese ambassador said.
Clinton and Hashimoto also planned to focus on relations with China and overtures to North Korea, McCurry said.

The summit follows a series of visits to Japan by top U.S. officials, including Gore, Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, Defence Secretary William Cohen and Gen. John Shalikashvili, chairman of the military joint chiefs of staff.
An administration official who asked not to be identified told Reuters the White House had hoped to have completed work on Foley's nomination to be the new U.S. ambassador to Japan before the summit.

But the focus of presidential lawyers on the controversy over the financing of Clinton's re-election campaign has diverted attention from other issues and has caused a logjam in the appointments process, the official said.
